I'm mapping out the grid coordinates to identify connected groups of 0s using 4-connectivity, so I can determine which zero-regions touch a 1 cell and need recoloring.

I'm noting the positions of the 1s in the grid, then tracing out groups of connected zeros to see which zero-clusters touch a 1 and which stay isolated. I'm walking row by row, checking adjacency between zero cells to build up these components.

Checking component C's neighbors — no adjacent 1s found, so it stays unrecolored. Then I check isolated cells (1,3) which also has no 1 neighbor, and move to (1,5) which connects to (2,5) and (2,4), tracing that region further.

No 1 nearby either. Then checking (2,9): it connects to (3,9), which chains down through a long path of zeros—(4,9),(5,9),(5,10),(6,10),(6,9),(6,8),(7,8),(7,7),(7,6),(8,6)—tracing this connected zero region to see where it leads.

Continuing to trace, I find the zeros keep branching through (8,7),(9,7),(9,6),(10,6),(10,5),(11,5),(12,5),(13,5),(13,7),(14,7), eventually hitting a 1 at (13,6)-(14,6), confirming this large connected region is adjacent to a mine. Also noting (10,10)=1 touches both (10,9) and (9,10), so this whole sprawling zero region is not safe to flag as empty.

Now I'm carefully listing every cell belonging to this component, tracing outward from (2,9) through the chain of connected zeros down to (15,7), and continuing to expand into new branches like (11,9) as I check neighbors that haven't been visited yet.

I keep following zero-value cells outward, adding (12,12), (11,12), (10,12), and (9,12) to the region before checking their neighbors and finding higher values that stop the expansion there. I also verify a few other adjacent cells along the boundary, then backtrack to check the (10,5) and (11,5) area for further connections.

Continuing the flood-fill, I check several more boundary cells around rows 12-15 and columns 4-8, confirming stopping points where values are nonzero, then move up toward rows 9-10 to trace connections through (9,6), (8,6), (8,7), and (7,6) — finding that (6,6) is another zero cell, so I add it and continue expanding upward toward (5,5), which also looks like zero.

Continuing to trace adjacency, I'm compiling the full set of grid cells belonging to region F, checking each candidate's neighbors before adding it to the list.

Moving to isolated cells: (3,3), (3,11) each have no matching adjacent value, so they stand alone. Then I find (4,1) and (4,2) are adjacent to (5,1), forming a small two-cell group G, and I start checking (4,15)'s neighbors next.

I'm tracing another connected component starting at (5,0), which links to (5,1), forming G2. Then (5,3) turns out isolated after checking all four neighbors. I'm now following a longer chain from (5,12) through (6,12), (6,11), (7,11), (7,10), (8,10), (8,9), tracing adjacency step by step to see where it connects into set F.

Wait, I realize I missed that (8,9) connects down to (9,9), which is already in F—meaning this entire cluster I was tracing actually belongs to F rather than being separate. I need to fold in the nodes I found: (8,9), (8,10), (7,10), (7,11), (7,12), (6,11), (6,12), (5,12), plus their additional neighbors (8,12), (7,13), (6,13), (4,12), (5,11), (5,13), and (8,8), all as part of F.

Then I'm checking more connections: (7,10) links left to (7,9), and (7,11) links down to (8,11), and (9,10) links right to (9,11)—all folding into F.

Now I'm finding a new cluster starting at (6,2) and (7,2), which connect together and form a separate group H, with neighboring values (5,2)=8, (8,2)=4, (7,1)=3, (7,3)=1, (6,1)=9, (6,3)=2 recorded around it.

Then I'm tracing another cluster near (6,15) and (7,15)/(7,14), checking their neighboring values.

Now I'm continuing that trace: (7,15) connects down to (8,15), which connects down to (9,15), forming a group I. Checking neighbors like (6,14)=8, (5,15)=6, (8,14)=4, (9,15)=4, and (7,13)=4, I find (8,13)=0 isn't actually connected since it only borders a 4-valued cell, so this cluster stays unchanged with no adjacent 1.

I'm moving on to examine another region starting around (8,0), (8,1), (9,0), (9,1), (9,2), (10,0), checking (8,0)'s upward neighbor.

Tracing this new group further, I find (8,0) is adjacent to a 1 at (7,0), so this whole cluster J = {(8,0),(8,1),(9,0),(9,1),(9,2),(10,0),(10,2),(10,3)} gets marked as adjacent to 1, after confirming connections through (9,2)→(10,2)→(10,3) and checking their neighbors don't introduce any breaks. Then I start checking (8,3), which also borders a 1 at (7,3), so I begin tracing its neighbors like (9,3) to build out that component too.

Tracing through this cluster of cells starting at (11,1), following adjacency links down through (12,1), (12,2), (13,2), (13,1), and finding it connects further via (13,0) to keep the component growing, labeling it N.

I keep expanding N to include (14,2), (14,3), (15,3), (15,4), checking neighbors along the way and confirming they merge into one connected region — no new nonzero neighbors break out, so this component collapses to a single group. I mark it as 1 and move on to check (10,10), which is nonzero, then start tracing another region near (13,9) and (14,9).

(14,9) and (14,10) both connect back through zero neighbors into the same region, so I fold them into that group too, giving another single component labeled 1. I check the surrounding cells like (15,11) and find it isolated on its own since all its neighbors are nonzero. Then I start following a new chain from (15,14) and (15,15) upward through zero cells at (14,15) and (13,15), continuing to trace how far this connected region extends.

I'm scanning nearby cells like (12,14), (11,13), (15,0), (14,0), and (12,0) for their values, checking whether any are isolated zeros or part of existing groups, then I go through row 13 cell by cell to log which values are already marked as part of the F region versus which are still unclassified.

Continuing this, I map out row 11 completely, noting each cell's value and marking several as belonging to group F, then I double-check (4,8) and scan through row 4 to identify zero cells at (4,1), (4,2) as part of group G, with (4,9) in F and (4,15) standing alone. I start working through row 2 similarly, tagging (2,2) as part of group E.

Now I begin constructing the actual output grid row by row: row 0 comes together with its mix of zeros, an 8, a 5, ones, a 9, and a 6, while rows 1 and 2 get filled in with their respective sequences of numbers, with specific cells like (2,9) confirmed as belonging to group F and assigned value 1.

Continuing row construction...

Row6 resolves to [9,9,1,2,8,1,1,3,1,1,2,1,1,5,8,0], then I move into row7, working through each cell's value and flagging entries that need to become 1.

Row8 finishes out as [1,1,4,1,7,4,1,1,4,1,1,5,8,1,4,0], and I'm starting to fill in row9's values now.

Still computing row values...

I finish rows 14 and 15, noting row15 has a cluster of zeros near the end—(15,11), (15,14), and (15,15) all landing on 0.

Then checking (8,8)'s neighbors, it links to (9,8) and (9,9), and since (9,9) is adjacent to a 1 at (10,9), that whole trio becomes 1. Similarly (10,6) and (10,7) connect upward to a 1 at (9,7), and I'm now tracing (10,12)'s zero-chain through (11,12), (11,13), and (11,14) to see what it connects to.

Continuing to check adjacency for each cell against its neighbors: (11,3),(11,4),(11,5) get marked 1 since they border a 1-cell, similarly (11,9) and (12,7) qualify, while (12,10),(12,11) have no adjacent 1 and remain 0. I'm now checking (13,5) against its four neighbors to determine its value.

Marking those remaining coordinates as 1, I now assemble the final grid row by row, filling in each cell's computed value.

Continuing through rows 11-14, I'm scanning for more zero clusters and repeated digit patterns in the grid.
